title: Chord Voicings
intro: A voicing is a particular arrangement of a chord's notes. The guitar's six strings and four fingers limit which voicings are playable, so guitarists use a standard vocabulary: open chords, barre chords, power chords, triads on three strings, and four-note seventh-chord shapes. Each is explained here by its intervals (see Chords (#/arts/music-theory/chords) for the chords themselves).

blocks.text: Open chords use open strings, so they ring and are easy to play, but they only exist in a few keys (C, A, G, E, D and their minors and sevenths). Their voicings are wide and often double the root: E major (022100) is E–B–E–G♯–B–E from low to high, three roots, two fifths and one third.
A barre chord lays the index finger across all the strings at one fret and forms an open-chord shape above it, so the shape becomes movable. The two most used:

items: E shape, root on string 6: major 1-3-3-2-1-1 (F at fret 1), minor 1-3-3-1-1-1, dominant 7 1-3-1-2-1-1, minor 7 1-3-1-1-1-1.
A shape, root on string 5: major x-1-3-3-3-1 (B♭ at fret 1), minor x-1-3-3-2-1, dominant 7 x-1-3-1-3-1, minor 7 x-1-3-1-2-1.
To play any chord, find its root on string 6 or 5 (see The Fretboard (#/arts/guitar/guitar-theory/fretboard)) and put the shape there.

blocks.alt: Six chord diagrams at the first fret: F, Fm and F7 using the E shape with a barre across all six strings, and B♭, B♭m and B♭7 using the A shape with a barre from string 5, roots in red and note names below.
blocks.caption: The two barre-chord families. Move any of them along the neck and the red root names the new chord.

blocks.text: A power chord (G5) is just root and fifth, often with the octave: 3-5-5-x-x-x. With no third it is neither major nor minor, which suits distorted electric guitar: distortion adds strong harmonics and intermodulation products, and a major or minor third under heavy distortion sounds muddy, while the 3:2 fifth stays clean. The same two-finger shape moves anywhere on strings 6 and 5.

Three-note triads on three adjacent strings are the guitarist's most flexible chords: clear, easy to move, and good for comping in a band. On the top three strings (G B E) C major has three inversions within the first 13 frets:

items: Second inversion G–C–E: x-x-x-0-1-0 (the top of the open C chord), or 12-13-12 on the top strings.

widget.title: C major triads up the top three strings

blocks.text: The same three inversions exist on every set of three adjacent strings; on sets that include the B string the shapes shift by one fret where they cross G–B, as always.

items: Drop-2: take a close-position seventh chord and drop the second-highest note an octave, giving a spread that fits four adjacent strings. Cmaj7 x-3-5-4-5-x is C–G–B–E (root, 5th, 7th, 3rd).

Drop-3: drop the third-highest note instead, with the string between the bass and the rest left out. Cmaj7 8-x-9-9-8-x is C–B–E–G (root, 7th, 3rd, 5th): the classic jazz-guitar root-on-string-6 voicing.

Shell voicings: root, 3rd and 7th only, the minimum that defines a seventh chord. G7 3-x-3-4-x-x (G–F–B), Cmaj7 x-3-2-4-x-x (C–E–B), Dm7 x-5-3-5-x-x (D–F–C). Freddie Green played big-band rhythm guitar almost entirely with shells, and they are the guitar version of the pianist's guide tones (see Jazz Harmony (#/arts/music-theory/jazz-harmony)).

blocks.title: Build a barre chord
blocks.text: Play C minor with an E-shape barre and with an A-shape barre.
solution: E shape: root C on string 6 is fret 8: 8-10-10-8-8-8.
A shape: root C on string 5 is fret 3: x-3-5-5-4-3.

blocks.title: Read the voicing
blocks.text: Name the chord and intervals of x-5-7-5-6-x.
solution: String 5 fret 5 = D3; string 4 fret 7 = A3; string 3 fret 5 = C4; string 2 fret 6 = F4. D–A–C–F: root, 5th, ♭7, ♭3, a D minor seventh (Dm7) in drop-2 voicing.
